# polyweave

> A Claude Code plugin for making a game's parts by declaring what each has to satisfy and
> letting a search find the parameters that satisfy it: 3D assets (geometry, surface and
> motion) and the pictures they start from, sound loops held to a seam, and the names and
> lines of the game's world. Levels are next, on the roadmap. It works on top of Blender,
> Godot and paid generators, on the developer's own machine, against files in their own
> repository: no GUI, no account, no hosted service.

**polyweave is Python under `src/polyweave`, installed as a Claude Code plugin from this
repository.** Its status is not typed here: the landing page states it, derived from
[`docs/ROADMAP.md`](https://github.com/alegauss/polyweave/blob/main/docs/ROADMAP.md),
whose every line, shipped or open, is a failure measured in a real project rather than a
feature somebody wanted;
[`docs/specs/`](https://github.com/alegauss/polyweave/tree/main/docs/specs) holds the
contracts that more than one of those lines depends on. Every measurement quoted on the
site or in this file was taken in **Cottony**, the game the backlog was drawn from, and
describes the cost polyweave exists to remove. None of it is a measurement of polyweave.

## For agents

This site answers a coding agent in files it can grep, not only in hydrated markup. Every
route has a Markdown twin beside it, the same page converted from the same render, with the
navigation, the footer and the call to action dropped. Read `<route>/index.md` instead of
the HTML: the landing page is
[`/index.md`](https://alegauss.github.io/polyweave/index.md). The full list of routes,
their twins and their byte sizes is in
[`manifest.json`](https://alegauss.github.io/polyweave/manifest.json).

## Why it exists

Generating a mesh is the cheap part. What is expensive is everything between *having a
mesh* and *knowing it is right*, and today that is a person changing one number at a time
and looking at a two-minute render. Cottony's render rig has fourteen tuned constants, and
every one of them was found that way. polyweave's premise is that the loop can be closed:
you state what the asset has to satisfy, and a search finds the parameters that satisfy it,
measuring against the reference rather than against an opinion.

## The mechanism

- **An acceptance spec** (`<asset>.accept.toml`) states what makes a render of the asset
  correct: a list of named predicates, each naming a measure from a closed vocabulary and
  stating one bound (`min`, `max` or `target`), plus a `[search.<param>]` block per
  parameter the search is permitted to move. A parameter the spec does not name is not
  searched.
- **Every predicate returns a margin, not only a verdict**: pass/fail *and* a value in
  [0, 1] for how comfortably it passed, normalised against the bound. A pure boolean gives
  a search a cliff and nothing to climb; the margin is what makes it converge.
- **The search** proposes values, bakes at the cheapest preview rung that can answer the
  question, measures, scores, and repeats. What comes back is the winning values, a contact
  sheet of the best handful side by side, and a trace of every sample it rejected with the
  predicate that rejected it.
- **A cache keyed on the inputs, the renderer and its version, and the seed** means a state
  the sweep has already rendered is not paid for twice.
- **The expected failure is a good one**: a search that satisfies every predicate and
  returns a render a person rejects tells you the *spec* is incomplete, which is the
  fastest way to find that out.

## The blocks

- **A — What a tool call costs the turn.** Anything over roughly two seconds returns a
  handle whose state is a file in `.polyweave/jobs/`, so it survives the session; a dead
  worker is `job.worker-gone` rather than a hang. Every operation asserts its own output
  before returning (a mesh has faces and finite bounds; a render is not a single uniform
  colour; a download's byte length matches and its sha256 is recorded), and a failed
  assertion is an error, never a warning. Errors are typed, namespaced and carry a `remedy`
  that is the call which closes them. An unknown field in any input is refused, never
  dropped. `describe()` returns each parameter's type, range and default read from the
  implementation; `capabilities()` says what this machine can actually do. Configuration
  resolves explicit argument → `polyweave.toml` → default, on every call.
- **B — Seeing the result cheaply.** A surface is read on a sphere in three seconds rather
  than on the final mesh in two minutes, and the rung is reported with every measurement,
  never inferred. A render returns its measurements in the same answer. A distribution is
  reported as a set (`p1`, `p50`, `p99`, mean, std) and never as a mean: Cottony's board
  matched the concept art's mean saturation to within 0.01 and looked plainly wrong,
  because the whole difference sat at the 99th percentile. Two runs of one unchanged scene
  differed in 29,696 pixels, none by more than 1/255, which is the noise floor any usable
  distance metric has to sit above.
- **C — The asset compiler.** The acceptance spec, the parameter search, the cache and the
  trace. This is the block the rest exists to make possible.
- **D — Fetching from a paid service without surprise.** The silhouette is checked against
  the reference drawing *before* a credit moves (a wide low cap was sent and a tall dome on
  a long stem came back, for thirty credits). The spend is bounded by a ceiling a person
  sets in the project config and a ledger against it, rather than by a question per fetch.
  What was bought is copied locally with its sha256 and a provenance sidecar, because the
  service deletes it after seventy-two hours. A fetched mesh is normalised into this
  project's axes, scale and origin, and a reference photograph's background is removed
  before it can be fused into the geometry.
- **E — One world with the engine.** Godot exits zero on a script error and non-zero on a
  clean quit, so the verdict is a line the script printed and no error in the log. A
  capture runs where there is no screen. The sprite grid is declared once and both sides
  read it. The runner's locale and settings are pinned.
- **F — Motion.** A skeleton, so a fetched mesh can be posed at all; clips rather than a
  second static render; curves as text a diff can show; and one source for both the 2D
  sprite frames and the 3D clip.
- **G — Geometry as a declaration.** A shape stated as data rather than written as a
  program, with a vocabulary read off what the existing assets already do (extruded
  outlines, crowned plates, radial arrays, annuli, boolean pockets), numbers the search can
  reach, a review before anything is built, and a way back to code for the shape no format
  can state.
- **H — Proof on a real game.** Cottony adopts the plugin, and the benchmark records how
  long a correct asset took before and after. Until that line ships, no number anywhere is
  a measurement of polyweave.

## Conventions, fixed once

- **Axes**: Y up, −Z forward, right-handed — the engine's convention, because the engine
  draws the result. Blender's Z-up and glTF's +Z-forward are converted on the boundary.
- **Scale**: one unit is one metre, unless the asset declares `pixels_per_unit`.
- **Origin**: the centre of the footprint, on the ground plane — the base of the
  silhouette, not the centre of the bounding box.
- **Colour**: sRGB in every authored document and every reported value. Linear values live
  inside a renderer and never in an interface.
- **Angles**: degrees in authored documents, radians nowhere a caller can see.
- **State**: `.polyweave/` inside the project, which belongs in `.gitignore`. A cache in a
  home directory is state a repository cannot review and a colleague cannot reproduce.
- **Formats**: TOML for documents a person authors or reads, JSON for records a machine
  writes. The split is about who edits the file, not about what is in it.

## Non-goals (governed, not accidental)

- **A graphical editor.** The caller is an agent in a terminal, so a surface that needs a
  person at a screen is one the agent cannot use at all.
- **Replacing Blender, Godot or the generative service.** Those three already do the work;
  what is missing is the loop around them.
- **Spending money on the agent's own judgement.** A fetch draws on a real balance, so the
  ceiling is a person's to set and the plugin's job is to make a spend bounded and visible.
- **One project's palette, rig or paths compiled in.** Cottony is the first consumer and
  not the specification; a default that cannot be overridden is a defect.
- **A hosted service or an account to sign into.** Everything runs on the developer's
  machine, because a plugin that needs an account is one that fails on the day the account
  does.

## Layout

- `docs/ROADMAP.md`, `docs/CHANGELOG.md`, `docs/IMPROVEMENTS.md`: governed by
  [roadkeep](https://github.com/alegauss/roadkeep) and written by that tool, not by hand.
- `docs/specs/`: ordinary documents, edited directly — the contracts more than one roadmap
  line depends on.
- `site/`: the public site (Vite + React + Tailwind). Its build emits this file, a Markdown
  twin per route and `manifest.json`, and it generates the roadmap counts and lines it
  displays from `docs/ROADMAP.md` through roadkeep, so the page cannot disagree with the
  file.
